title: Poets and Pancakes
summary: In this humorous memoir, Asokamitran recalls his years at Gemini Studios, a famous film company in Madras in the 1940s. He paints amusing portraits of the make-up department, the office boy, the gifted Subbu, the legal adviser and the visit of an English poet, gently satirising the film world, its hierarchy and its politics.

notes.heading: About the author
notes.html: Asokamitran (1931–2017), pen name of J. Thiagarajan, was a celebrated Tamil writer who worked at Gemini Studios for about fourteen years. The chapter is an excerpt from his memoir My Years with Boss, ‘Boss’ being S. S. Vasan, the studio’s founder.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: The author describes the make-up room, where heavy Pancake make-up was used to turn decent-looking actors into monsters under hot lights, and a strict hierarchy decided who painted whom. He sketches the office boy who wished to be a poet or director, the multi-talented Subbu, the legal adviser whose blunder ended an actress’s career, and the studio’s story department. He recounts the visits of the Moral Re-Armament army and of the English poet Stephen Spender, whose speech nobody in the studio understood. Years later the author realises Spender’s link with the book The God That Failed.

notes.heading: Detailed summary
notes.html:
The make-up department. Pancake was the brand of make-up the studio bought in truckloads. The make-up room, on the upper floor of a building said to have been Robert Clive’s stables, was lit with huge mirrors and incandescent lights, so it felt like a furnace. The department was a model of national integration, headed by a Bengali and staffed by people from many states. A strict hierarchy ruled: the chief make-up man did the hero and heroine, his assistants did the second leads, and the office boy daubed paint on the crowd players.

The office boy. He was not really a boy but a man in his forties who had joined hoping to become a star, screenwriter, director or lyricist. He was bitter at being left behind and blamed Subbu for his failure, often unloading his frustration on the author.

Subbu. Kothamangalam Subbu was the Boss’s No. 2. Loyal, cheerful and endlessly creative, he could solve any film-making problem and offer many ways to shoot a scene. He was a poet, novelist and fine actor, though he never wanted lead roles. He was generous to friends and family. Yet, being close to the Boss, he drew envy.

The story department and the legal adviser. The story department had writers and poets, and a lawyer officially called the legal adviser, though people called him the opposite. He once switched on a recorder during an actress’s outburst on set and played it back to her; she was so shocked that she never acted again. Dressed in trousers, tie and sometimes a coat among khadi-clad colleagues, he seemed an isolated, slightly helpless figure.

Politics and the MRA visit. Most at Gemini were khadi-wearing Gandhians, but none was politically active. They were anti-communist and thought communists godless people. In 1952 the Moral Re-Armament army, a group opposing communism, visited the studio with about two hundred people and staged plays like Jotham Valley and The Forgotten Factor. Their presentation influenced Madras theatre for years, and Gemini’s films borrowed their sunrise and sunset scenes.

Stephen Spender’s visit. Later, an Englishman, editor of a British periodical, came to the studio. He spoke to the staff in an accent no one understood, and they were puzzled about why he had been invited. Years afterwards the author, having won a prize in a short-story contest run by The Encounter, learnt that its editor was Stephen Spender, the poet. He then realised why the Boss had invited him: Spender had contributed to The God That Failed, a collection of essays by writers disillusioned with communism.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• Humour and satire: gentle mockery of studio life, hierarchy and pretensions.
  • Unfulfilled ambition: the office boy’s frustration reflects many who never rise.
  • Talent and loyalty: Subbu’s dedication to his master.
  • Politics and culture: anti-communist sentiment and the cultural influence of visiting groups.
  • Communication gaps: the Tamil studio staff and the English poet could not understand each other.

notes.heading: Character sketches
notes.html:
Subbu: versatile, imaginative and loyal; a problem-solver who made film-making seem easy, a good host and a generous man, though some saw him as a sycophant.

The office boy: an ageing man with literary and film ambitions, frustrated and envious, a tragicomic figure.

The legal adviser: educated but tactless; his single act destroyed an actress’s career and earned him an ironic nickname.

The author: a self-deprecating observer whose job was to cut newspaper clippings; his tone is wry and affectionate.

notes.heading: Title justification
notes.html: ‘Pancake’ refers to the make-up brand used at Gemini Studios; ‘poets’ refers to the writers and poets of the story department and to Stephen Spender. The title neatly sums up the two worlds of the studio: glamour and creativity, often mixed with absurdity.

notes.heading: Message and values
notes.html: The chapter encourages us to view life with humour, to respect genuine talent, and to recognise how ambition and politics shape workplaces. It also shows the importance of understanding one’s audience when communicating.

questions.q:
Read the situation and answer: The author describes how the make-up men, using bright lights and heavy paint, could turn any reasonably good-looking person into a hideous, puffy-faced monster.
(a) Why were the lights necessary in the make-up room? (1)
(b) What is the tone of the description? (1)
(c) What does it suggest about the make-up men? (1)
(d) Name the device used in calling actors ‘monsters’. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Bright lights were needed to apply make-up accurately for shooting.

(b) Humorous and mildly satirical.

(c) That they used make-up excessively and without subtlety.

(d) Hyperbole.

questions.q: Why was Subbu considered a fine actor though he never played lead roles?
questions.answerHtml: Subbu had a natural talent for acting and could make any role convincing. He played supporting parts with such skill that he outshone the lead actors. He never aspired to be a hero, preferring to help the Boss and the studio behind the scenes.

questions.q: Why was the legal adviser given an ironic name by others?
questions.answerHtml: A legal adviser is expected to prevent trouble. Instead, his tactless act of recording an actress’s outburst and playing it back to her ended her career. Because his advice caused harm rather than help, people called him the opposite of a legal adviser.

questions.q: What does the author mean by saying the studio staff were ‘anti-communist’ though not politically active?
questions.answerHtml: Most employees were khadi-clad Gandhians who supported the Congress in spirit but took no part in politics. They vaguely disliked communism, believing communists were godless people who rejected family and tradition. Their opposition was a matter of belief rather than action.

questions.q: How does Asokamitran use humour to describe life at Gemini Studios? (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Asokamitran’s memoir is full of gentle, self-mocking humour. He describes the make-up room as a furnace where good-looking actors were turned into monsters, and calls the department a model of national integration because people of all states worked there together. The strict hierarchy, in which the office boy painted the crowd players with his ‘brush’, is presented with mock seriousness.

He laughs at himself too, describing his own job of tearing newspapers as one that others considered doing nothing. The frustrated office boy who wanted to be a great poet, and the legal adviser whose ‘legal’ advice ended an actress’s career, are portrayed with ironic affection.

The climax of comedy is the visit of the English poet whose speech nobody understood, and whose identity the author discovered only years later. Through such irony, understatement and exaggeration, he exposes the absurdities of studio life without bitterness.

questions.q: Write a character sketch of Kothamangalam Subbu. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Kothamangalam Subbu was the Boss’s No. 2 at Gemini Studios and one of its most gifted figures. He was extraordinarily creative: whenever the producer faced a difficulty in filming, Subbu could suggest several ways of shooting a scene. He made film-making look easy.

He was multi-talented, a poet whose work had a popular touch, a novelist and a remarkable actor in supporting roles, though he never sought the limelight. He was also loyal, totally devoted to the Boss and willing to put his talents in his service.

Subbu was generous and charitable. His home was always open to friends and relatives, and he was kind to all. Yet his closeness to the Boss and his success made some people envious; the office boy, for instance, blamed Subbu for his own failure. Overall, Subbu emerges as a cheerful, warm and brilliant man who was the real driving force of the studio’s story department.
